paragraphs.source_en: Shelters are usually designated for specific members of the society; the initiation shelters for young boys or girls and elders, and other shelters for dead people or for rain-makers but there are also "pagan" shelters for everyone who wishes to paint for their personal needs. The paintings in all shelters may be periodically repainted and new images added.

units.source_en: Shelters are usually designated for specific members of the society; the initiation shelters for young boys or girls and elders, and other shelters for dead people or for rain-makers but there are also "pagan" shelters for everyone who wishes to paint for their personal needs.
The paintings in all shelters may be periodically repainted and new images added.

paragraphs.source_en: The images are associated with specific rituals which indicate their function or significance. Thus, the depiction of certain kind of masks refers inevitably to the ritual they are used in, and they may have been depicted in secret shelters in which these masks were stored when they were not in use (Le Quellec 2004). In the shelters used for the storage of masks the Dogon also undertake the circumcision during boys' initiation rituals and after each ritual the paintings already existing on the wall are repainted (Palau Marti 1957).

paragraphs.source_en: In northern Nigeria, among the Marghi speaking groups, the role of rock paintings in shelters is to document a boy's successful rite of passage. These sites are often associated with lithophones which are used in initiation ceremonies. The female initiation shelters are documented in Malawi and the paintings they contain are said to be made by girls during the initiation ceremony in the same shelters (Le Quellec 2004). In Mozambique, the inhabitants of the Chauremba mountains bring offerings and practise rituals in the ancestors' shelters, and they make paintings which represent the dead people's souls. The portrait of an important deceased person is painted on a rock sacrificed to him or her by the Wamia people in Tanzania (Ten Raa 1969).
